rows.verified: Workplace transport risk assessments must include vehicle and pedestrian movements, loading, unloading and less frequent transport tasks.
Mapping vehicle and pedestrian movements helps identify interaction points and opportunities to reduce contact.
Pedestrian routes and vehicle routes should be separated wherever reasonably practicable.
Sites should avoid reversing where possible and consider one-way systems, safe crossings, suitable lighting and safe loading areas.
Work vehicles should receive daily safety checks and planned preventive maintenance based on time, mileage and manufacturer guidance.
Work vehicles must be suitable for their purpose and maintained mechanically sound, with attention to brakes, steering, tyres, visibility and warning systems.
Employers should ensure drivers understand vehicle hazards and precautions and should monitor vehicle use.
Site traffic control should combine suitable vehicles, road layout, markings, signs, procedures and training.
Workplace-transport controls depend on site layout, traffic volume, vehicle type, pedestrian flows, visibility, reversing, surfaces, loading activity, driver competence and maintenance.
Workplace-transport evidence is site-, vehicle-, task- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level collision probability.
Motor vehicle repair risks include mechanical repair, elevated vehicles, tyres, hot work, emissions, electrical systems and hazardous substances.
Two-pack isocyanate paints can cause occupational asthma and dermatitis and require effective exposure control.
Powered sanding and discing should use built-in extraction or local exhaust ventilation to control fine dust.
Welding and hot-work fume should be controlled using suitable extraction, especially in enclosed or confined areas.
Vehicle-repair premises should separate pedestrians and vehicles, control speed, reduce reversing and provide safe customer reception areas.
Safe vehicle repair needs controls for inspection pits, tyre inflation, work below raised vehicles, fire and explosion and hybrid or electric vehicles.
Roadside repair and recovery must protect repair workers and other road users.
Motor vehicle repair businesses should use a suitable risk assessment and sector guidance covering the activities and equipment present.
Motor-repair controls depend on vehicle technology, repair task, lifting method, tyre or pressure system, paint or chemical, hot work, workshop layout and worker competence.
Motor-vehicle-repair evidence is vehicle-, task-, workshop- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury or illness probability.
